Pityriasis alba is common in children/adolescents, often with faint scaling and ill-defined borders, and may enlarge gradually but typically resolves spontaneously — plausible but less likely without age or atopy context. Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation follows skin injury or inflammation (e.g., eczema, psoriasis), often with history of preceding erythema or scaling — possible, though no such history was provided. Tinea versicolor causes fine-scaled, hypopigmented (or hyperpigmented) patches, usually on seborrheic areas, and may slowly enlarge; KOH exam would confirm, but scaling is often subtle or absent in hypopigmented variants. Nevus depigmentosus is a stable, congenital, non-progressive hypopigmented patch — inconsistent with the reported progressive enlargement over months, making it unlikely as the primary diagnosis."}
